subject: Public Park Showers
comment: I'm looking to see if there is any solution to proper hygiene for the homeless. I know that public parks do not have showers but they still have public stalls. I'm hoping that if I suggest something I hope to be taken seriously. A lot of public opinion when it comes to people experiencing homelessness is the lack of incentive and ultimate laziness of people who do not want to work. I know this personally because I was homeless for a year from 2019-2022. The lack of access for a shower led me to vulnerable situations where I ended up getting assaulted by multiple people because I was looking for the basic necessities to live at least with some dignity. My situation is not unique or uncommon. Many people will turn to survival sex or have been sexually or physically assaulted because they are looking for a place to get physically clean. Recently a woman was sexually assaulted by a man who offered her a place to shower in his apartment. Ejiek A Al Alwani was a registered offender, offering homeless addicted women a safe place to clean up where he would end up raping them, threatening them, and then getting away with it. He has repeatedly raped multiple women, but was only charged for this in late October of this year. I know this happened in South Salt Lake, however it is not an isolated incident. The ability to access a shower should be a basic human right in my opinion. It also would solve issues for many people who are trying to get jobs, who have menstrual cycles, who deal with addiction and have soiled themselves, and so many other reasons. One solution I hope you will consider is the access to a camping shower. They are relatively inexpensive and only need water added to the bag. I do know that many people steal things like hand sanitizer out of the public bathrooms, but it would provide security that wouldn't be an issue. It is a possible solution for women like the one I mentioned above. And there are plenty of park staff as well as people who could fill it once someone had used it. If you would be kind enough to respond, I'd greatly appreciate it. If not, I am more than happy to discuss it with one of the potential mayors running in Salt Lake City who are more than happy to listen to what I have to say. - Andria Teifer.

subject: Public Comment Regarding the Proposed Rezone of Fleet Block
comment: Good evening, I would like to submit a comment regarding the proposed rezone of Fleet Block. I want to thank Council Member Fowler for noting during the Work Session today that in order to retain community trust, the Council must uphold promises that have been made to the families of those who are memorialized in the murals. I urge the Council to center the expressed concerns and wishes of those families in any plans to redevelop Fleet Block. I especially urge you to incorporate preservation of the murals into any proposals for what to do with the block. I am disheartened to read that "the walls where the murals were painted are hard to save because of the material" in the official information at https://fleet-block-rezone-slcgov.hub.arcgis.com/. I would think that with the technological advances in building and engineering today, a way to preserve the murals could be found. Please include preservation methods for the murals in any RFP you may issue about redeveloping the block. I also support the suggestion made during the Work Session today that the RFP include requirements that potential partners have strong social justice/community partnership/diversity, equity and inclusion credentials, above and beyond what would be required in a normal RFP. Anyone who works on redeveloping this block must be committed to respecting and making manifest the community's wishes about what to do with the space. Fleet Block is sacred to many community members, and its powerful purpose as a place to mourn, come together, share emotions, and heal must be maintained in any future plans for the block. Thank you. ~ Regards, Levy Woodruff

This epidemic is slowly killing Salt Lake and has this city inline to be the next Portland and Seattle by 2024.

subject: Neighborhood Byways
comment: Dear Councilwoman Fowler, I am a resident of District 7 who mainly gets around by cycling and transit. I recently learned about Salt Lake City's proposed Neighborhood Byways program. The city's online survey on the matter closed before I could get to it, so I'm writing you to voice my support for the program. Kensington Avenue, in particular, strikes me as so close, yet so far, from being an optimal east-west cycling route. I live on the northern edge of Sugar House, and I have occasionally cycled or walked along Kensington to get home. It is largely pleasant, but frequent unprotected intersections with busy streets detract from this significantly. Perhaps worst of all is 700 East, an extremely dangerous 5troad that forces me to zigzag across when there is a gap in traffic, or else cross on 1700 South, at a still very hostile intersection to anyone outside a car. Protected crossings and traffic-calming devices could make Kensington a vibrant east-west corridor, from the East Bench to Ballpark. In addition to the proposed Neighborhood Byways, I urge the city to implement better traffic-calming and cycling infrastructure on 1700 South, the street where I live. The death of one of my neighbors by a driver back in May made clear to me that I am not safe on the sidewalk in front of my house. With 1700 South being a largely residential street, I fail to see why it should serve as a corridor for so many cars going 30+ mph. This makes it an unwelcoming environment for its own residents to walk, cycle, or even back their car out on it. Thank you for taking the time to read my thoughts. From your friendly constituent, Sam Thomas
